en: The Theravāda Vinaya Mahāvibhaṅga:
The Section on Offenses Entailing Expiation (Pācittiyakaṇḍa)
The Chapter on Jewels, 86.
The Training Rule on the Needle Case.
At that time, the Buddha, the Blessed One, was dwelling among the Sakyans at Kapilavatthu in the Nigrodha Monastery.
Now at that time, a certain ivory-worker had invited the monks,
saying, "To whichever venerable ones there is need for a needle-case,
I [will provide] a needle-case. At that time, the monks were requesting many needle-cases.
Those who had small needle-cases requested large needle-cases;
those who had large needle-cases requested small needle-cases.
Then that ivory-worker, while making many needle-cases for the monks, was unable to make other merchandise for sale; he could not even support himself, and his wife and children suffered.
People criticized, complained, and grumbled:
"How can these ascetics, followers of the Sakyan, not know moderation and request so many needle-cases?
This man, while making so many needle-cases for them, is unable to make other merchandise for sale; he cannot even support himself, and his wife and children suffer."
The bhikkhus heard those people grumbling, complaining, and criticizing.
Those bhikkhus who were of few desires... [and so on]... they grumbled, complained, and criticized:
"How can these bhikkhus, lacking moderation, request many needle-cases?"... [and so on]...
“Is it true, monks, that the monks do not know moderation and request many needle cases?
“It is true, Blessed One.
The Buddha, the Blessed One, rebuked them … [as before] …
"How indeed, monks, could those foolish men, not knowing moderation, request many needle-cases?

This, monks, does not lead to the confidence of those without confidence... And thus, monks, you should recite this training rule: 'If a monk should have a needle-case made, it shall be made according to the measurement; that is, the measurement of the Buddha’s span. Should he have one made exceeding that measurement, there is an offense of wrong-doing.'"
“Whosoever, however, a bhikkhu should have a needle-case made of bone, or of ivory, or of horn, it is an offense of expiation involving breaking.
Whosoever, however: whosoever of such a kind... [and so forth].
"Bhikkhu" ...
[as before] ... this is the "bhikkhu" intended in this context.
"Bone" means:
Whatever bone there is.
"Tusk" (danta) refers to the tusk of an elephant.
"Horn" means any kind of horn whatsoever.
"Should have made" means...
Whether one does it oneself or causes another to do it, there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa) for the preliminary effort.
Upon obtaining [the materials] and having broken [the vessel], a confession of an offense entailing expiation (pācittiya) must be made.
If one completes by oneself what was begun by oneself, there is an offense of expiation.
If one completes what was begun by oneself with the help of others, there is an offense of expiation (pācittiya).
If one completes what was begun by others with one's own help, there is an offense of expiation.
If one completes what was begun by others with the help of others, there is an offense of expiation.
If one makes it or causes it to be made for another purpose, there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa).
If one uses what has been obtained as something made by another, there is an offense of wrong-doing.
There is no offense—
The toggle-pin,
the fire-drill,
and the spindle.
An ointment box,
an ointment stick,
and a perfume container.
[The exceptions are: for one using a water-wringer,
for one who is insane,
and for the first offender.
The fourth training rule concerning the needle-case is finished.
